xgCpq_w0cn8.title: Arabic Tafsir of Surat al-Qasas: Guidance, Quraysh's Fear for Their Livelihood, and Ingratitude, Verses 56-58
xgCpq_w0cn8.one_line: You cannot control anyone's guidance; Quraysh rejected truth to protect trade and alliances; ingratitude for blessings slowly destroys communities.
xgCpq_w0cn8.summary: The sheikh returns to verse 56 to separate the sin from the sinner: the Prophet testified that a man repeatedly flogged for drinking loved Allah and His Messenger, and forgave Hatib's leaked letter, so we must not curse people or attack scholars' integrity, only critique their ideas with evidence. Guidance is not ours in amount, kind or timing; trying to control children, spouses or anyone else brings only frustration, while our role is to encourage, model and make faith attractive, and to guard our own guidance. Abu Talib and Abu Lahab show that even the Prophet could not guide his own family. Verse 57 records Quraysh admitting the message was guidance yet fearing they would be 'snatched from their land': their pacts with the tribes, idols placed at the Kaaba and protected caravans depended on idolatry. He likens this to rulers who drop their pretence on Palestine and insists truth must be upheld whatever it costs. Allah answers that He, not idols or treaties, made the barren sanctuary safe and supplied, so do not confuse the door of provision with the Provider. Verse 58 warns that communities ungrateful for their livelihood lose it gradually. He ends by asking whether we would leave a job for Allah, so we do not judge Quraysh but learn from them.

outline.heading: Guidance as part of our relationships
outline.gist: Muslims lose sleep over relatives' guidance partly because they evaluate people; the surah aims to cure judging others and looking down on them.

outline.heading: Separate the wrong from the wrongdoer
outline.gist: Forbidding a sin differs from judging, exposing or shaming the sinner.

outline.heading: The drinker who loved Allah and His Messenger
outline.gist: When a companion cursed a man flogged repeatedly for drinking, the Prophet stopped him and testified that the man loved Allah and His Messenger.

outline.heading: Punishment without contempt
outline.gist: That testimony frees a person from hypocrisy; the Prophet said the woman of Ghamid's repentance could cover the people of Madinah, and never taught contempt for sinners.

outline.heading: Critique a scholar's ideas, never his integrity
outline.gist: Calling a stance wrong is fine; slandering a scholar, even one dead a thousand years, is uncivilised and unprophetic.

outline.heading: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's letter
outline.gist: He leaked the Prophet's plan to Quraysh to protect his family; the act was wrong, but once his reason was heard he was pardoned as a veteran of Badr.

outline.heading: You do not even know your own family
outline.gist: Every scene in al-Qasas proves our judgements wrong; even an identical twin does not know what goes on inside the other.

outline.heading: Guidance is not yours in amount, kind or timing
outline.gist: You cannot decide how much, in what form or when anyone is guided; guide, teach, encourage and model, but you do not guide.

outline.heading: Stop trying to control people
outline.gist: If Allah gave people choice, who are you to force them? Accepting you cannot control children or spouse brings relief; do what is within your power.

outline.heading: Whoever tries to control others is disgraced
outline.gist: Only Allah is al-Muhaymin, and He chose to give each person free choice in belief.

outline.heading: Abu Talib and the Year of Grief
outline.gist: The Prophet begged his uncle for one word; the grief of losing a loved one outside faith is unlike losing Khadijah, whom he will meet in paradise.

outline.heading: Guard your own guidance
outline.gist: No one knows when guidance may be taken away, which is why we ask for it at least seventeen times a day; guidance is what counts in the end.

outline.heading: Present guidance on a golden plate
outline.gist: Make the deen attractive through character, speech and understanding, then accept that Allah decides.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab, Nuh's son and Ibrahim's father
outline.gist: Abu Lahab made his sons divorce Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum, who waited years to remarry; if prophets could not impose guidance on family, neither can you.

outline.heading: Recitation with grammar and tajwid notes
outline.gist: The conditional jazm, the kasrah to avoid two sukuns, the merged noon in 'numakkin', and the mushaf's spelling conventions for Hafs via al-Shatibiyyah.

outline.heading: Quraysh finally admit it is guidance
outline.gist: Lies have short legs, as with rulers who dropped their pretence of supporting Palestine; 'they follow their desires' was a verdict told only to the Prophet.

outline.heading: Why the People of the Book were praised
outline.gist: The companions were starting to see goodness only in themselves, as the Jews and Christians claimed to be Allah's beloved; Muslims must not repeat that claim.

outline.heading: 'Not by your wishes'
outline.gist: Neither Muslims' nor the People of the Book's wishes decide salvation; it is not a servant's place to tell his Lord who enters paradise.

outline.heading: 'We would be snatched from our land': Quraysh's pacts
outline.gist: Quraysh hosted the tribes' idols at the Kaaba in exchange for safe passage for their caravans, a system tawhid would end.

outline.heading: Tribes fought for custody of the Kaaba
outline.gist: Serving the Kaaba meant honour and trade; Thaqif and Hawazin seized it repeatedly and Fihr and Qusayy won it back.

outline.heading: The War of Fijar and 'you do not understand geopolitics'
outline.gist: The young Prophet shot arrows defending Makkah; Quraysh's reply resembled today's big words used to belittle people who hold to principle.

outline.heading: The truth is clear: no compromise
outline.gist: Palestine is stolen land whose people were expelled and its sanctities violated; upholding truth may cost you everything, but you may not compromise on it.

outline.heading: Quraysh's offers to the Prophet
outline.gist: Alternate years of worship, drop the poor followers, take money, kingship or wives: he refused, because the one with the truth is strong.

outline.heading: 'Did We not establish a safe sanctuary for them?'
outline.gist: Revealed shortly before the hijrah; Allah, not idols or treaties, made the barren valley safe and drew all fruits to it.

outline.heading: A civilisation without a river
outline.gist: Civilisations rise by rivers and fertile land, yet Allah sustained Makkah for millennia, gave it Zamzam and placed vast energy reserves beneath the region.

outline.heading: The door of provision is not the Provider
outline.gist: Your job or shop is a door of provision; confusing it with the Provider is exactly Quraysh's error.

outline.heading: Batar: ingratitude for one's livelihood
outline.gist: The Prophet honoured blessings however small; a man who eats, digests and lives safely and is still unsatisfied is ungrateful, unlike the cancer patient, a former chef, who could not eat.

outline.heading: Comparison breeds ingratitude; destruction by Allah's ways
outline.gist: Envying others' cars and houses; this destruction is not a thunderbolt but the slow working of Allah's laws, which is why dwellings remain.

outline.heading: Blessings slip away gradually
outline.gist: Gratitude increases provision while greed and ingratitude strip it bit by bit, until it is too late to recover.

outline.heading: 'We were the inheritors': loss for Allah is compensated
outline.gist: Islam later made the Hajj greater than before; whatever is left for Allah is replaced with better, and even if not, wealth may not be used against the truth.

outline.heading: Would you give up your livelihood for Allah?
outline.gist: Quraysh's refusal was about money and their children's future; we too compromise principles to avoid angering people.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab: 'stop this mouth'
outline.gist: Banu Hashim, long poor but noble, had only lately gained wealth, and Abu Lahab would not risk his new trade.

outline.heading: Do not judge Quraysh; learn from them
outline.gist: As al-Miqdad warned, you do not know what you would have done; never let wealth, status or fear make you compromise the truth.

outline.heading: Only the truth remains
outline.gist: Great civilisations become tourist ruins, while those who stood with the truth are remembered; Allah inherits everything and you will explain your choices to Him.

outline.heading: Outro
